stem: How does Garland's West differ from the West in Currier and Ives prints and dime novels?

stimulus.source_note: Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' Main-Travelled Roads (1891). Public domain. Text verified against Project Gutenberg (eBook #2809) and Original Sources.
stimulus.text:
Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' in Main-Travelled Roads (1891) (ellipses mark omissions):

"It was the last of autumn and first day of winter coming together. All day long the ploughmen on their prairie farms had moved to and fro in their wide level fields through the falling snow, which melted as it fell, wetting them to the skin all day, notwithstanding the frequent squalls of snow, the dripping, desolate clouds, and the muck of the furrows, black and tenacious as tar."

"'I didn't like the looks of the country, anyhow,' Haskins said. 'I was ust t' northern Ingyannie, where we have lots o' timber 'n' lots o' rain, 'n' I didn't like the looks o' that dry prairie.'"

options.text: Garland's West has no farmers in it at all
options.misconception: Background: Garland's farmers fill the story; the ploughmen are the whole scene.

options.text: Garland's West is a place of easy wealth and adventure
options.misconception: Background: Garland's farmers are soaked, cold, and in debt; easy wealth belongs to the novels, not to his stories.

options.text: Garland's West is a place of mud, debt, and backbreaking work
Garland's West is empty of people
options.misconception: Background: Garland's West is crowded with ploughmen, families, and neighbors; it is not empty.

rationales.A: Background: Garland's farmers fill the story. The ploughmen are the whole scene.
rationales.B: Background: Garland's farmers are soaked, cold, and in debt. Easy wealth belongs to the novels, not to his stories.
rationales.C: Garland shows ploughmen soaked in snow. Background: the family is later driven out by grasshoppers, and the popular Currier and Ives prints showed a pleasant, bucolic West, and Garland answers them with mud and debt.
rationales.D: Background: Garland's West is crowded with ploughmen, families, and neighbors. It is not empty.
rationales.general:
Picture two Wests side by side: a bright print on a parlor wall, and a man soaked behind a plough.
1. Read Garland's scene. Snow, mud, and cold. Background: the family is later driven out by grasshoppers.
2. Ask what the prints showed instead. Background: A pleasant, bucolic farming life, tidy and contented.
3. Name the difference. Garland's West is work and debt; the prints' West is a picture.
Remember: when a story and a picture disagree, trust the one that smells of mud.
